title: She Dreamt of Cirque du Soleil. In Ahmedabad, a New York Mother and Her Daughter Won Gold and Bronze at the World Yogasana Championships.
excerpt: India swept the inaugural championships with 102 gold medals from 79 countries. But a mother-daughter pair from the US, and 12-year-old prodigies from Delhi and Bengal, told the bigger story.
body:
Kemi Blake dreamt of becoming a contortionist. She left New York for Las Vegas to train at the Cirque du Soleil academy. Her daughter Kimani, 16, learned gymnastics and wanted to be a professional dancer. Both found yoga. And this week, in a sprawling arena in Ahmedabad built for the 2030 Commonwealth Games, the mother and daughter made history together.

Kemi won gold in the Back Bend individual category. Kimani took bronze in the Junior Artistic Individual event. They are believed to be the first American mother-daughter pair to medal at an international yogasana championship.

"I never thought of coming to compete here," Kemi told SAI Media. "I thought I was not good enough to compete against the Indian players. But a fellow Romanian player who follows my Instagram page encouraged me. And some coaches from India encouraged me too."

They were competing at the inaugural World Yogasana Championships, held at the EKA Arena from June 4 to 8, an event that may one day be remembered as the moment an ancient Indian practice officially became a global competitive sport. Organised by Yogasana Bharat in association with World Yogasana and the Indian Olympic Association, the championships drew 522 athletes from 79 countries — and India, predictably, dominated.

The hosts finished with 114 medals, including 102 gold. Japan came second with three gold, three silver, and five bronze. Argentina's lone athlete, Nabila Barraza, won two gold and three silver to place third. Nepal claimed 52 total medals — one gold, 36 silver, and 15 bronze — finishing fifth. Uzbekistan rounded out the top tier with 25 medals.

But the numbers only tell part of the story. What stood out was India's depth. Junior and sub-junior athletes — some as young as 10 — contributed 46 of India's 102 gold medals. Leading the next generation were 14-year-old Ishika Guchhait from Delhi and 12-year-old Sanwita Banerjee from Durgapur, West Bengal, who won gold in the sub-junior girls' rhythmic pair event.

"Winning 46 gold medals at this level underscores the effectiveness of our grassroots development and coaching systems," said Jaideep Arya, Secretary General of World Yogasana. "The emergence of talents like Ishika and Sanwita is a testament to years of nurturing at the school and academy levels."

India fielded 122 athletes across six age categories — from Sub-Junior (10-14 years) through Senior C (45-55 years) — competing in traditional yogasana, artistic single, pair and group, rhythmic pair, and specialised flexibility and balance events. Thirty-one of the 79 participating nations won at least one medal. Ten countries won gold.

The championships were supported by India's Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Ministry of Ayush, the Sports Authority of India, and the Gujarat state government — a coalition that signals how seriously India views yogasana's pathway toward Olympic recognition. Ahmedabad, which will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games, was chosen deliberately as a statement venue.

For the Indian diaspora, the competitive yogasana movement carries a layered significance. Yoga studios in New York, London, Toronto, and Sydney are fixtures of urban life. Millions of NRIs practice some form of yoga daily. But the transformation of yogasana from wellness routine to medal sport — with formal rules, judged events, age categories, and national teams — represents something new: India exporting not just a cultural practice, but a sporting discipline it intends to own on the world stage.

The Middle East is taking notice. Oman won medals, Jordan's Maya Alostath earned bronze, and officials believe the Gulf region — with its large South Asian expatriate communities and growing government investment in wellness — could become a significant pipeline for competitive yogasana.

Kemi Blake, the gold medallist from New York, put it simply: "I started yoga to improve flexibility for my performances. But it gave me purpose and stability. I started eating right, sleeping on the floor, and my outlook towards life changed."

Her daughter Kimani, standing beside her with a bronze medal, is 16 and already planning her next championship.
